title: The Diwali permit, 1734
hookLine: Bhai Mani Singh arranged a Diwali gathering at Amritsar, was unable to pay the tax, and was executed

lines: BHAI MANI SINGH ASKS FOR A PERMIT.
cards: Diwali at Amritsar. Lamps on the water, the Harmandir glowing, Sikhs coming in from every direction to bathe, to listen, to see each other's faces. In the hunted years, that gathering had become impossible.
So a man who had served the Guru himself went to the governor in Lahore and asked, formally, for a permit.
He was Bhai Mani Singh, the same Sikh who, tradition says, had once settled the quarrel of the two slips in the pool. The governor named a price, and Bhai Mani Singh agreed to pay it.

teach.h: A FEE FOR A DIWALI GATHERING.
teach.b: Tradition says the plan was simple.

teach.h: A TRAP: HE TELLS SIKHS NOT TO COME.
teach.b: Sikhs would come for Diwali, offerings would be made, and from those offerings Bhai Mani Singh would pay the fee he had promised.
But word reached him that the governor meant to use the gathering as a trap, to send soldiers among the crowds.
So Bhai Mani Singh did the one thing that would ruin his own position: he sent messages telling the Sikhs not to come. Think about the cost of that choice.
He saved the people, and he guaranteed that the money would not be there. Few came. The offerings fell short.
He was arrested and taken to Lahore, where, tradition says, he was offered his life if he would give up his faith. He refused. And the sentence was terrible: to be cut apart, joint by joint.
Sikhs remember those who died this way.

In the Ardas, the standing prayer said at the close of Sikh services, the sangat recalls those who were cut limb from limb and did not give up their faith, and tradition places Bhai Mani Singh among them.
He was not only a martyr. Tradition remembers him as a scholar and scribe, a man who had served Guru Gobind Singh closely and cared for the Harmandir for years.
A whole life of careful, patient service ended in one refusal. The permit was a piece of paper. What he kept was not on paper.

how: Sikhs remember Bhai Mani Singh at Diwali and in the daily Ardas, which recalls those who were cut limb from limb rather than give up their faith; Gurdwara Shaheed Ganj in Lahore marks the place tradition gives for his death.

o: the spring harvest festival in Punjab
the festival of lamps, kept at Amritsar
a permit to gather, sold by the governor

s: Bhai Mani Singh could not pay because he kept the money
he warned the Sikhs away to save them, so the offerings never came.
he warned the Sikhs to stay away, knowing he then could not pay
tradition says he chose their safety over the fee he had promised.

games.q: you're Bhai Mani Singh. you've promised the governor a fee from the Diwali offerings, and now you learn the gathering is a trap. what do you do?
o: let the gathering go ahead so you can pay.
warn the Sikhs not to come, even though you won't be able to pay.
games.why: tradition says he sent word for the Sikhs to stay away. the money never came, and he was arrested and executed in Lahore.

practice: Bring to mind one promise you've made that matters to you, to a person, to God if you pray, or to yourself; maybe it's been slipping, or costing more than you expected.
Don't judge it; just hold it in front of you and feel its weight. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Diwali, the festival of lamps. Bhai Mani Singh promised a fee for a Diwali gathering at Amritsar; when he warned Sikhs away and could not pay, he gave his life rather than his faith.
